summary: This memo describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board. It is a periodic snapshot listing protocols and their maturity levels, and it was replaced by RFC 1500. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a report card for Internet rules, saying which ones were final, which were drafts, and which were just ideas. It is historic and a newer report card replaced it.

questions: what were the official internet protocol standards in 1993
how does a protocol become an internet standard
subtitle: The standardization process and maturity levels for Internet protocols as of 1993.

tldr.problem: The Internet protocol suite evolved without a formal categorization system, and developers needed to know which protocols were official standards, which were being tested, and which had been superseded.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB created a two-dimensional classification system: maturity levels (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Historic, Informational) and requirement levels (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended). Protocols advance through the standards track only via IAB and IESG approval.
tldr.outcome: This memo became the authoritative status report for all Internet protocols. It was issued periodically and superseded by RFC 1500.

today: RFC 1410 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 1500 in August 1993. The Internet standards process continues under the framework defined in RFC 1310 (updated by later RFCs), with the Internet Society and IETF maintaining the standards track for new protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1410 is the Internet Architecture Board's official status report on protocol standardization. The IAB maintains this memo as an authoritative reference for determining the state of every Internet protocol: which are official standards, which are in development, which are experimental, and which have been superseded.

The RFC describes two independent categorization systems for protocols: maturity level (how far along the development path a protocol is) and requirement level (how important it is for different types of systems to implement it). This memo lists all protocols in each category and explains the path by which a protocol can move through the standardization process.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is like a report card for Internet rules. It says which rules are final decisions, which are still being tested, which are old and no longer used, and which ones everyone must follow versus the ones that are optional.

sections.title: How Protocols Are Classified
sections.content:
Each protocol occupies a cell in a two-dimensional matrix. The first dimension is the maturity level or state: Standard (official), Draft Standard (being considered), Proposed Standard (candidate), Experimental (research use), Informational (for reference only), or Historic (superseded or unused). The second dimension is the requirement level or status: Required (must implement), Recommended (should implement), Elective (optional), Limited Use (special circumstances), or Not Recommended (avoid).

A new protocol typically enters the matrix in the Proposed Standard state with Elective status. Only protocols that are officially on the standards track (Proposed, Draft, or Standard states) can move between cells under IAB and IESG approval. The RFC notes that a protocol's requirement level may change as it matures, and the IAB may also predict what status a protocol will have when it reaches Standard state.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols are sorted two ways: how ready they are (final, testing, idea, old, or reference) and how important they are (must-have, should-have, optional, special-use, or avoid). A rule starts as an optional idea and can move up to being a required final rule.

sections.title: The Standards Track Progression
sections.content:
The RFC defines a formal progression path, called the standards track, that a protocol must follow to become an official Internet Standard. A protocol enters the track only on the recommendation of the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) and with approval by the IAB.

The progression has minimum waiting periods: a protocol must spend at least 6 months as a Proposed Standard before being considered for Draft Standard, and at least 4 months as a Draft Standard before being elevated to Standard. Before promotion to Proposed Standard, there must be at least two independent implementations; promotion to Draft Standard generally requires demonstrated interoperability between multiple implementations. Protocols can also be assigned to the Experimental or Historic states, either as a side track or as a destination when a protocol is deemed unsuitable for standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new Internet rule is proposed, it must go through stages: first as a test idea (where two groups build it), then as a draft (where people make sure two copies work together), then as official. Each stage takes at least a few months. Some rules are too early or too broken, so they stay experimental or become historic instead.

sections.title: The Protocol Landscape in 1993
sections.content:
As of March 1993, the RFC lists 43 Standard protocols across the Internet core and networks. These include the fundamental protocols: IP (Internet Protocol), ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), UDP (User Datagram Protocol), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), and the major application protocols like Telnet, FTP, SMTP, and Domain Name System (DNS). The memo also lists 11 Draft Standard protocols, over 100 Proposed Standard protocols, numerous Experimental protocols like Directed ARP and DNS-based IP routing, and a growing list of Historic protocols from earlier RFCs.

The RFC notes that protocols are organized by category: standard Internet protocols, network-specific protocols (defining how IP runs on different physical networks), Telnet options (collected for reference), and MIB standards for network management. Recent changes section details new protocols and how older protocols were promoted or moved to Historic status.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1993, TCP and IP and DNS were official rules. Newer ideas like multicast routing and various ways to run IP over different networks were being tested. Some older rules from the 1980s were no longer used and marked as historic.

sections.title: Status and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1410 is marked Historic and was superseded by RFC 1500, published in August 1993. The IAB issued this standards status memo periodically (approximately quarterly as noted in the introduction) to keep the community informed of current standardization status. Each edition captured a snapshot of the protocol suite's evolution at a point in time.

The memo was also the authoritative reference for determining the official RFC number for each protocol (since protocols were often updated across multiple RFCs) and contained contact information for the IAB, IETF, IRTF, and IANA. It served as the hub for understanding Internet protocol governance and the formal process by which new protocols could enter and advance through the standardization track.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo was replaced by a newer one the same year. The IAB issued these status reports a few times per year so everyone would know which rules were final and which were still in the works. It also said who to contact if you had questions about the process.
